notes.title: Start here: Formbricks and its side effects
notes.body:
Formbricks is an open-source survey platform: a Next.js app with Prisma over Postgres (`formbricks/apps/web`), an embeddable survey SDK (`formbricks/packages/surveys`) and shared packages such as `packages/cache`. The study course lives in `formbricks/fabledocs/upskill/`.

This quest is about what happens around a response, not inside the form. Read two files of the course:

1. `03-architecture-and-patterns/04-side-effects-async-and-reliability.md`: an inventory of every way the app touches the outside world, graded for reliability.
2. `09-reference/risk-register.md`: the same weaknesses as a table of risks, each with evidence, a suggested test and a confidence level.

Several line numbers in these guides point at older versions of files (for example the responses route), so search for the function name when a line does not match. The register itself says every row is a starting point, not an accusation: read the cited code and decide for yourself.

notes.title: Concept: check-then-act races and fail-open guards
notes.body:
A **check-then-act** race happens when code reads a value, decides, and writes, while another request does the same in between; both decisions rest on a value that is already stale. Test three places against that definition: for each one, decide whether it fits, and what two concurrent requests would see.

- `handleQuotas` in `apps/web/modules/ee/quotas/lib/utils.ts`: what is counted, what is compared with `quota.limit`, and when the links are written. Note whether any lock or conditional update is used.
- The backup-code branch of `authorize` in `apps/web/modules/auth/lib/authOptions.ts`: follow the codes from decryption to the `prisma.user.update`, and read its `where`.
- `withCache` in `packages/cache/src/service.ts`: count how many times `fn` would run if many requests miss the same key together.

A guard that cannot decide either **fails open** (lets traffic through) or **fails closed** (refuses it). Read `checkRateLimit` in `apps/web/modules/core/rate-limit/rate-limit.ts`, list every return statement with its condition, and decide which kind it is. Then read the guide's browser-to-server paragraph to see which side of the system retries.

notes.title: Why a missing CRON_SECRET breaks the pipeline silently
notes.body:
`sendToPipeline` is an `async` function whose first statement is `if (!CRON_SECRET) throw new Error(...)`. A throw inside an async function becomes a rejected promise, and the `.catch` in the function belongs to the `fetch` that never starts. The responses route calls `sendToPipeline(...)` without `await`, so nobody handles that rejection. The response was already written and the route still returns success, but no pipeline event runs, and Node reports an unhandled rejection.

- *A 500*: the route does not await the call, so the throw cannot reach it.
- *Empty x-api-key*: the throw happens before the request is built.
- *Caught by the fetch .catch*: that catch is attached only to the fetch promise.

excerpts.quote: if (!CRON_SECRET) { throw new Error("CRON_SECRET is not set"); }

notes.title: Why a 500 from a webhook goes unnoticed
notes.body:
`fetch` resolves its promise whenever a response arrives, whatever the status code; it rejects only for network failures, aborts and similar errors. The delivery chain returns the response and never checks `response.ok`, so a 500 is treated like success. The `.catch` that logs 'Webhook call ... failed' runs only for a thrown error. Nothing retries either way.

- *Retried three times*: there is no retry in the route.
- *Logged as failed*: the log runs only on rejection, and a 500 is a resolution.
- *Webhook disabled*: no code disables webhooks after failures.

excerpts.quote: .catch((error) => { logger.error({ error, url: request.url }, `Webhook call to ${webhook.url} failed`);

notes.title: Which webhooks an event reaches
notes.body:
`getWebhooksForPipeline` asks Prisma for webhooks in the environment whose `triggers` array has the event, and whose `surveyIds` either contains this survey or is empty. An empty list therefore means 'all surveys'. A webhook limited to other surveys, or not subscribed to this trigger, is skipped.

- *Every webhook*: the trigger filter is part of the query.
- *Only explicit survey ids*: the empty-list branch also matches.
- *Whatever surveyIds says*: a non-empty list without this survey excludes the webhook.

excerpts.quote: triggers: { has: event }, OR: [{ surveyIds: { has: surveyId } }, { surveyIds: { isEmpty: true } }],

notes.title: Which webhook headers are always sent
notes.body:
For every delivery the route builds `webhook-id` from a new `uuidv7()` and `webhook-timestamp` from `Math.floor(Date.now() / 1000)`, which is seconds. Only `webhook-signature` is conditional: it is added inside `if (webhook.secret)`. These are the Standard Webhooks headers; because the id is created per call, a retry would need to reuse it for consumers to dedupe, which is why the guide calls it groundwork.

- *Signed with an empty key*: no signature without a secret.
- *No headers without a secret*: id and timestamp are set unconditionally.
- *Signed with the API key*: no API key is involved.

excerpts.quote: const webhookMessageId = uuidv7(); const webhookTimestamp = Math.floor(Date.now() / 1000);

notes.title: Why the timeout uses AbortSignal
notes.body:
A `Promise.race` between `fetch` and a timer only decides which promise the caller sees first; the losing fetch keeps running with its socket open. Here that matters because the route later destroys or drains a per-request dispatcher, and the comment says a still-open fetch would deadlock `dispatcher.close()`. `AbortSignal.timeout(5000)` cancels the underlying request, so nothing is left hanging.

- *Edge runtime*: the comment names no runtime limitation.
- *A self-retry*: an aborted request is not retried.
- *Rejecting other webhooks*: each delivery has its own promise; the issue is the open socket.

excerpts.quote: a Promise.race would only reject the wrapper while the fetch keeps the socket

notes.title: Why webhook redirects are not followed
notes.body:
Before sending, the route validates the webhook URL and resolves it, refusing private and internal ranges. A redirect would send the request to a new URL that was never validated, for example an internal service. Setting `redirect: "manual"` stops that bypass. Self-hosters who set `DANGEROUSLY_ALLOW_WEBHOOK_INTERNAL_URLS` keep the old follow behaviour, for consistency with their opt-in.

- *Confirm by a 302*: the comment is about security, not confirmations.
- *undici cannot follow*: it can; the route chooses not to.
- *Timeout restarts*: the timeout is not the reason.

notes.title: Why two simultaneous responses can both pass a full quota
notes.body:
`handleQuotas` counts existing screened-in links for each quota (leaving out the current response), and treats the quota as full only when that count is at least `quota.limit`. Then it writes the links. Two transactions running together both count 0 for a limit of 1, both decide 'not full', and both write screened-in links. Nothing locks the quota or makes the write conditional on the count, which is why risk R2 suggests a conditional counter update or `FOR UPDATE`.

- *Row lock*: no lock is taken.
- *Neither screened in*: each sees zero others, not one.
- *Unique-constraint error*: the two links are for different responses.

notes.title: Why a repeated finish event does no harm to auto-complete
notes.body:
For each `responseFinished` event the route compares the survey's response count with `survey.autoComplete` and, when the count has reached it, calls `updateSurvey` with status `completed` and queues an audit event. A second delivery of the same event repeats the same update. Because the target state is the same, the repeat changes nothing. The guide uses this as the example of a race with an idempotent effect being tolerable.

- *Rejected as stale*: no deduplication exists.
- *Only above 100*: the comparison is `>=`.
- *Admin confirmation*: the close is automatic.

notes.title: Why the rate limiter lets traffic through without Redis
notes.body:
`checkRateLimit` has three ways to allow a request without counting it: rate limiting disabled, no Redis client (`logger.debug('Redis unavailable')`), and any error in the Redis call, whose catch reports to Sentry and returns `ok({ allowed: true })`. The comment states the choice: fail open, for availability over perfect limiting. It applies to every namespace, including login, which is risk R3.

- *Refuse logins*: nothing returns `allowed: false` without a Redis count.
- *An error result and 503*: the function returns `ok(...)`.
- *Allow after a retry*: there is no retry loop.

excerpts.quote: Fail open - allow request if rate limiting fails

notes.title: Why concurrent cache misses all hit the database
notes.body:
`withCache` reads the key; on a miss it awaits `fn()` and then writes the result. Each request does this independently. Twenty requests that miss at the same moment each run `fn`, so a hot key's expiry turns into twenty identical database queries: a cache stampede. A single-flight map or a lock would let one call refresh while the others wait.

- *A Redis lock*: the class has a lock helper, but `withCache` does not use it.
- *An in-process promise map*: that is the suggested fix, not current code.
- *Stale-while-revalidate*: there is none; an expired key is a miss.

excerpts.quote: const fresh = await fn(); await this.trySetCache(key, fresh, ttlMs);

notes.title: Why one backup code can log in twice
notes.body:
The code path decrypts the whole `backupCodes` blob, finds the submitted code with `indexOf`, sets that slot to `null`, and writes the re-encrypted blob back with `prisma.user.update({ where: { id: user.id } })`. The update is not conditioned on the old value. Two logins that run at the same time both read the old blob, both find the code, and both succeed. Risk R13 suggests a row per code deleted with a count check, or an update conditioned on the old ciphertext.

- *Redis*: the codes live in the user row.
- *Reusable by design*: the code sets the slot to null to burn it.
- *A row lock*: the read takes no lock.

excerpts.quote: backupCodes[index] = null; await prisma.user.update({ where: { id: user.id,

notes.title: Why the browser side is at-least-once
notes.body:
Losing a respondent's answers is unacceptable, so the survey SDK keeps responses in a `ResponseQueue` that retries failed sends and persists them offline (`packages/surveys/src/lib/response-queue.ts`). The server has no retries of its own. A unique constraint on single-use links stops a retried submission from creating a second response there. Beyond the server, the pipeline is at-most-once.

- *A BullMQ worker*: the guide says there is no queue or worker fleet.
- *The pipeline route*: it sends outward; it does not resend to the server.
- *A Postgres trigger*: none is involved.
